L’imposition de visas aux Mexicains fait: Visa requirement for Mexicans raises fears of more dangerous border crossings
Depuis le 29 février, Ottawa oblige de n: Since Feb. 29, Ottawa has once again required Mexican travellers to present a visa at the border
Viviana a dû fuir le Mexique en raison d: Viviana had to flee Mexico because of threats to her life. She is worried about Ottawa’s new decision to reimpose visas on Mexican nationals for people in her situation. Illustration: Nia E-K
Depuis le 29 février, Ottawa oblige de n: Since Feb. 29, Ottawa has once again required Mexican travellers to present a visa at the border. According to experts and activists based in Montréal, the measure raises fears of the worst for those among them who are trying to file an asylum claim in Canada.
Conséquence de la nouvelle mesure ? Les: The consequence of the new measure? Travel authorizations granted up to Feb. 29 have been cancelled. People affected by the cancellation must start their travel process over by applying for a visa. Exemptions have been announced for international students and temporary agricultural workers.
La première chose qu’on remarque quand o: The first thing you notice when you talk with Viviana is her great energy and her relaxed style. She arrived by plane from Mexico two years ago, and the activist for the rights of women and girls in her home country is very worried about her loved ones.
Elle réagit vivement à la nouvelle impos: She reacts strongly to the new visa requirement, an obligation that had been lifted in 2015 by the Trudeau government: “It seemed a bit unfair to me, a bit inhumane, that they did it this way! And that people are missing their flights, losing money – people who had maybe saved up and who couldn’t afford to come here to claim asylum.” Two years ago, Viviana claimed asylum in Canada, fearing for her life.
« Je me souviens avoir dû rassembler de: “I remember having to scrape together money for my flight and leave the country immediately because my safety, my life, were seriously threatened. If my flight had been cancelled, I would have kept facing a great risk,” she says.
Viviana estime qu’elle n’a pas eu le cho: Viviana believes she had no choice but to leave Mexico, where she received threats because of her work defending women’s rights. Along with several feminist collectives, she took part in the search for missing women.
« Tout ce travail nous a placés en confl: “All that work put us in conflict with different groups. In my case, it was the military, who didn’t like what we were doing. There were threats and direct persecution against me and my organization,” she explains.
« Des militaires sont même venus chez mo: “Soldiers even came to my home and beat me.” Although she tried to hide out with comrades in other states of the country, she was tracked down.
L’exil est devenu sa seule porte de sort: Exile became her only way out.
Nina est une femme dynamique qui se préo: Nina is a dynamic woman who cares about the fate of everyone. A volunteer at the Centre des travailleurs migrants, she fights against violations of the labour rights of people without status in Montréal and elsewhere in Quebec.
Quand on la rencontre, le bureau est ple: When we meet her, the office is full, and she is coordinating the arrival of people seeking employment advice. In her view, this visa requirement for Mexicans reinforces certain stereotypes about Latin Americans, namely that they are all violent and linked to organized crime.
« Alors que la vaste majorité des gens q: “Whereas the vast majority of the people who come here are victims of violence who are only looking to integrate,” she says.
Dans les bureaux du Comité pour les droi: In the offices of the Comité pour les droits humains en Amérique latine (CDHAL), over coffee, Rosalinda Hidalgo sharply criticizes the return of visas for Mexicans: “I think it’s a racist, discriminatory and exclusionary decision.” She believes the decision is part of a broader tightening of Canada’s immigration laws, following, for example, the closure of the Roxham Road crossing.
« Cette décision est troublante parce qu: “This decision is troubling because it cannot guarantee the asylum policy, which must be maintained for those who seek it,” says the CDHAL director.
« Je pense qu’on va aggraver la situatio: “I think we are going to worsen the risks for migrants. You don’t control migration like this; people will come by other routes.”
Joint par téléphone, Carlos Rojas, fonda: Reached by phone, Carlos Rojas, founder and director of Conseil Migrant, an organization that supports migrants with precarious status, deplores the decision.
« Fermer Roxham et imposer le visa, ça n: “Closing Roxham and imposing the visa does nothing at all. Measures like these increase the business for smugglers and human traffickers, and they increase human rights violations,” he says flatly.
« C’est comme si on donnait aux trafiqua: “It’s as if we were giving traffickers permission to do whatever they want.”
« Ça me préoccupe parce que les personne: “It worries me because people who want to migrate will look for another way, even an illegal one, to come here,” Viviana also believes. <l1>The case of Ana Karen Vasquez-Flores, a pregnant Mexican woman who drowned while trying to cross the Canadian border illegally into the United States</l1>, is a sad illustration of Viviana’s words.
Depuis 2015, 7 118 demandes d’asile dépo: Since 2015, 7,118 asylum claims filed by Mexicans have been accepted in Canada. At a press conference, Immigration Minister Marc Miller said Ottawa is reimposing the requirement because Mexicans are making “abusive” asylum claims. He said 17 per cent of all asylum claims submitted in Canada in 2023 came from that country.
À des milliers de kilomètres d’Ottawa, l: Thousands of kilometres from Ottawa, the organization Kino Border Initiative works with migrants at the border between Mexico and the United States, in the state of Arizona. During a conference <l1>organized by the Center for Migration Studies</l1> on the different faces of migration at the border between the two countries, Johanna Williams, executive director of Kino Border Initiative, reported a marked increase in Mexican migrants fleeing violence.
« Nous travaillons avec des personnes bl: “We work with people stranded in Nogales,” she says. Her organization estimates that in 2023, 76 per cent of the people in its shelters were Mexican and that half of them came from the state of Guerrero, in southwestern Mexico.
« 83 % des personnes accueillies par Kin: “83 per cent of the people welcomed by Kino reported that violence and persecution were the main reasons for their migration. It’s a rising trend that we are seeing.”
Au banc des accusés ? Une fragmentation: What’s to blame? A fragmentation of the violence of gangs that increasingly control villages and wage war against each other. Recently, the organization’s staff heard the story of a family that fled their village. It was caught in the crossfire of two rival gangs: the one that controlled the village and another that wanted to take it from them.
Ce type de situation, de plus en plus fr: This type of situation, which is increasingly common, marks a shift in Mexico, she says. <l1>Since 2018, more than 30,000 people have been murdered every year</l1> in the country, which is facing a crisis of kidnappings, disappearances and other violent crimes. “Civilians are bearing the brunt,” reports the Global Conflict Tracker, an interactive guide that gathers information on ongoing conflicts, citing violence by organized crime, but also by the state.
Joanna Williams (troisième personne à pa: Joanna Williams (third from the right) works in Arizona and Mexico. She has seen an increase in the violence experienced by Mexican nationals fleeing their country.
Les femmes font aussi tragiquement les f: Women also tragically bear the brunt of this violence, as femicides are a problem pointed out by many organizations, both national and international. For example, in 2020, 3,723 violent deaths of women were recorded in Mexico, <l1>according to Amnesty International</l1>.
« Dans cette guerre contre le narcotrafi: “In this war against drug trafficking, it’s the civilian population that is the victim of this violence. Women and girls have been truly vulnerable for several years,” says CDHAL director Rosalinda Hidalgo.
« La violence dans notre pays a beaucoup: “Violence in our country has increased a lot and, unfortunately, there is a lot of corruption. The police, who are supposed to protect you, are instead complicit with criminal groups,” adds Vivana, some of whose colleagues campaigning for women’s rights are still missing to this day.
Rosalinda insiste sur un autre aspect de: Rosalinda stresses another aspect of welcoming Mexican nationals. Because <l1>Canada causes problems, notably in the mining sector</l1>, it has a “moral obligation” to welcome people suffering from the consequences of the operations of companies with questionable practices. “Extraction by Canadian mining companies causes internal displacement, but also environmental contamination. It also causes human rights violations,” she notes.
Une position qu’appuie Carlos Rojas. « O: Carlos Rojas supports this position. “We bring in Mexicans and Guatemalans to pick our vegetables in our fields. Then we resell most of that agricultural production to the United States,” he says. “So we bring people here, we exploit them here… to trade with the United States.” Although agricultural workers are exempt from the visa requirement under Canada’s new measure, the fact remains that Mexicans are welcome only if they are willing to take on difficult jobs.

Rojas tente de faire ado: Since 2018, Mr. Rojas has been trying to get the principle of a humanitarian corridor between Mexico and Canada adopted. “It would involve setting up offices in the camps for people at the border between Mexico and the United States, but also pretty much everywhere in that country,” he proposes. Such an approach has been implemented in some refugee camps, notably in Syria, to help nationals of that war-torn country flee to Canada.
M. Rojas vient d’ailleurs d’envoyer une: Mr. Rojas has in fact just sent a letter to Foreign Affairs Minister Mélanie Joly asking her to consider this option following the recent imposition of visas on Mexican nationals.
Johanna Williams, au cours de la confére: Johanna Williams, in the talk she gave in the United States on the plight of Mexicans, points out that most of them want to stay in their communities, but that certain problems, including violence, force them to flee.
Assise et pensive, dans le bureau du Col: Seated and pensive in the office of the Collectif bienvenu, Viviana says she is enjoying her new life, even though her journey has been difficult. “Mexico is a very dangerous country, very dangerous for a woman, for an activist,” says the woman, who hopes with all her heart that her comrades who will need to flee the country won’t have to take great risks to get to Canada.
« Le gang qui avait le contrôle de l’end: “The gang that controlled the area organized a meeting that all the villagers had to attend.
